label: Vector Fields
notes: This chapter follows one object, a vector field, through four increasingly structural viewpoints: a smooth section, a coordinate expression, a derivation of smooth functions, and an element of a Lie algebra. Keep that arc in mind, because every later result is one of those viewpoints talking to another across thirty pages of theory.

label: Smooth Sections of TM
notes: Stress that a vector field is not a loose bag of arrows. It is a section: a smooth right inverse of the bundle projection that selects exactly one tangent vector over each point. The circle is the cleanest picture because tangency is visible, and the section appears as the horizontal graph v equals one in bundle coordinates.

label: The Space X(M)
notes: Here we collect all smooth vector fields into the single space written script X of M. Emphasize the two algebraic structures living on it simultaneously: a real vector space and a module over the ring of smooth functions, so coefficients are themselves functions, not just constants. This module view is what makes local frames meaningful later.

label: Local Frames and Coframes
notes: A frame is an ordered tuple of fields that is a basis of the tangent space at every point of its domain. Coordinate frames are the prototype, but not every manifold admits a global frame. Mention parallelizability and the hairy ball theorem so students see that the existence of nonvanishing fields is a real topological obstruction.

label: Coordinate Expressions
notes: Drive home that one geometric field has many coordinate faces. The rotation field minus y d-x plus x d-y is exactly the angle field in polar coordinates. Changing coordinates changes the component functions, never the underlying assignment. Flag the domain warning: the polar expression is not a single chart at the origin, so smoothness must be checked chart by chart.

label: Fields as Derivations
notes: This is the conceptual hinge of the chapter. A smooth vector field acts on smooth functions by directional differentiation, and that action is linear over the reals and satisfies the Leibniz product rule. The theorem is that derivations of the smooth function algebra are exactly the smooth vector fields, which gives us a coordinate-free identity for a field.

label: Xf and Level Curves
notes: Use the contour picture to make the derivation tangible. Where an arrow skims along a level curve of f, the directional derivative X f is near zero; where the arrow cuts across contours, X f is large. This visual makes the abstract operator concrete and previews why brackets measure a genuine geometric failure to commute.

label: F-related Fields
notes: Introduce relatedness carefully: X and Y are F-related when the differential of F sends X at p to Y at F of p, for every p. Pushforward of a field needs single-valuedness over fibers. A diffeomorphism has unique preimages so its pushforward always exists; a general smooth map can fail, and we will see that failure explicitly.

label: Pushforward Failure
notes: The fold map t to t squared is the cautionary example. The two preimages of a positive target point push the same source field to opposite target vectors, so no single target field can represent the pushforward there. Contrast that with the circle parametrization, where relatedness holds cleanly. The lesson: fibers with multiple points break naive pushforward.

label: The Lie Bracket
notes: Define the bracket as the commutator X Y minus Y X of the two derivations. The surprise is that although each composite is second order, the second-order parts cancel and the bracket is again a first-order operator, hence a genuine vector field. Present the coordinate formula and verify it on the partial-x, x partial-y example giving partial-y.

label: X(M) as a Lie Algebra
notes: Collect the bracket's algebraic properties: it is bilinear, antisymmetric, and satisfies the Jacobi identity, so the space of smooth fields is an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra. Then state naturality: F-related fields have F-related brackets. This is the structural payoff, because it means brackets survive pushforwards, restrictions, and homomorphisms exactly when the hypotheses hold.

label: Left-Invariant Fields
notes: Left-invariant fields are determined by their value at the identity, so the Lie algebra of a Lie group is finite-dimensional, isomorphic to the tangent space at the identity. Use the affine group of the line as the smallest visible nonabelian model: two basis fields a partial-a and a partial-b with the single nonzero bracket equal to E two.

label: Recap and Failure Modes
notes: Close by replaying the arc and naming the failure modes that keep students honest. A field is a smooth section; acting on functions makes it a derivation; relatedness controls pushforward and is fragile off diffeomorphisms; the bracket makes the field space a Lie algebra; and left-invariant fields shrink that algebra to finite dimension for a Lie group.
